_note: Golden numbers that BOTH tools must produce from tests/data/sample_alarm_log.csv.
The browser tool and the Python tool implement the same analysis twice, in two
languages. Fourteen functions are near-literal translations of each other, and
until this file existed their agreement was enforced by a sentence in
CONTRIBUTING.md and nothing else. They had already drifted twice.
So this file is the referee. tests/test_cross_tool.py reads it and checks the
Python tool against it. tests/browser/run.mjs reads the same file and checks the
browser tool against it. A change that moves one tool and not the other fails in
whichever suite was not updated, which is the point.
The numbers were worked out from the fourteen rows the 30 day window keeps, by a
standalone script that shares no code with either tool, then confirmed in both.
Do not regenerate them from either tool's output: a golden file produced by the
code it checks proves nothing. If a case here genuinely needs to change, change
it by hand and say in the commit message why the old number was wrong.
Every duration in the sample is a whole or half hour, so these compare exactly
and any drift shows up as an obvious number rather than a rounding argument.

cases.name: whole window, all hours
why: Fourteen rows totalling 18.5 hours of duration. Two overlap, 10:00-14:00
and 12:00-15:00 on the 10th, so wall clock drops to 16.5. In range loses
another half hour: the last row starts at 20:00 on the 21st, the exact
moment the window closes, so none of its duration is inside the report.

cases.name: day shift, 06:00 to 18:00
why: Eleven rows start between 06:00 and 18:00, including the overlapping
pair, so wall clock is 2 hours under attributed. In range happens to
match wall clock here. That is the ordinary case, not a rule.

cases.name: night shift, 18:00 to 06:00
why: Three rows: 22:00 on the 20th, 03:00 on the 21st, 20:00 on the 21st.
The first two are the same night on two different dates, which is the
whole reason the filter wraps. No overlaps, so wall clock equals
attributed. In range is half an hour less: the 20:00 row starts as the
window closes. Thirty-one blocks rather than thirty because the night
in progress when the window opened counts its tail.

cases.name: second shift, 14:00 to 22:00
why: Keep this case. It is the only one where in-range downtime is LARGER
than both other numbers, and it is the clearest demonstration of what
the third number is for.
Only three faults start on second shift, worth 2.0 hours, and half an
hour of that is lost because the 20:00 row runs past the window's end.
So 1.5 hours comes from rows on this shift. The other hour comes from a
fault that started at 12:00 on the 10th, on FIRST shift, and was still
running at 14:00. It put the tool on the floor for an hour of second
shift, and only the in-range number counts it.
This is why no test may assert that in-range is bounded above by wall
clock or by attributed. It is bounded by the clock, and by nothing else.

_note: Properties that must hold for ANY split of the day, not only the cases
above. Both suites assert these as well as the fixed numbers, because a law
catches a class of bug that a table of numbers can miss.

shifts_partition_rows.description: Rows land in exactly one shift, so the parts add up to the windowed rows.

three_shifts_partition_rows.description: The same over three eight-hour shifts, one of which wraps past midnight.

shifts_partition_in_range.description: In-range downtime splits across shifts and adds back up to the whole window. Neither of the other two downtime numbers does this, which is the reason the third one exists.

three_shifts_partition_in_range.description: The same law over three shifts.

shifts_partition_covered_time.description: The covered hours split the same way the downtime does.

in_range_never_exceeds_covered.description: The tool cannot be down for longer than the report is long. True of in-range alone; attributed and wall clock are not bounded by the clock, and neither bounds in-range. See the second-shift case.
